title: San Juan to Asunción: the Pampa Read as Desert, and the Schoolhouse Brought Home
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: San Juan, the house on the calle del Norte
stops.campa: A low adobe house of one room and a fig tree, raised by his mother Paula Albarracín with wool she wove herself on a loom set under the branches. Doña Paula's husband, José Clemente Sarmiento, is a militia captain of small means and large enthusiasms; the boy is their fifth child and their first son to live. He is named Faustino Valentín, and will call himself Domingo Faustino. He learns to read at four. In this house the poverty is total and the ambition is unembarrassed, and the two never afterward separate in him.
suggested_refs: The Casa Natal de Sarmiento in San Juan, the loom and the fig tree, first national historic monument of Argentina
sources: Museo y Biblioteca Casa Natal de Domingo Faustino Sarmiento

stops.name: San Juan, the Escuela de la Patria
stops.campa: The new republic, five years old and at war, opens schools before it opens roads. In San Juan the Escuela de la Patria is run by two Buenos Aires teachers, the brothers Ignacio and José Rodríguez, on the mutual method, with a discipline of medals and disgraces. The boy attends every day for six years and is never once absent, never once punished, and is made First Citizen of the class. He will remember the room exactly for the rest of his life, and will spend that life trying to reproduce it, multiplied, across a continent.
suggested_refs: The Escuela de la Patria of San Juan, the first republican school he sat in and the model of every one he later built

stops.name: San Juan, the six scholarships not drawn
stops.campa: Buenos Aires offers six places at the Colegio de Ciencias Morales to be filled by lot among the provinces. San Juan draws its names; his is not among them. There is no appeal and no second list, and the province has nothing else to give a poor boy with a memory like his. He is ten. The wound never closes: everything he afterward builds, the normal schools, the national colleges in every province, the eight hundred schoolhouses of his presidency, is a machine designed so that the lottery need never be run again.
suggested_refs: The Colegio de Ciencias Morales of Buenos Aires, the education he was not given

stops.name: San Francisco del Monte de Oro, the first school
stops.campa: His uncle, the friar José de Oro, is exiled to a hamlet in the hills of San Luis, and the nephew goes with him. In a mud-walled room the two open a school: the friar teaching theology and politics to the boy, the boy, at fifteen, teaching letters to seven pupils, some of them older than himself. It is his first classroom and his first command. He rings the bell, he sets the copybooks, he keeps order. The teacher of a nation is made here, in a place with no road to it, out of a priest's disgrace.
suggested_refs: The chapel and school of San Francisco del Monte de Oro, San Luis, where he first taught

stops.name: San Luis, the prisoner who taught his jailers
stops.campa: The unitarian cause collapses in Cuyo after the Rodeo de Chacón, and the young officer is taken and held on an estancia outside San Luis, at the mercy of a federal family that could have him shot on a whim. He does what he will always do with a locked room: he turns it into a school, teaching the household's sons their letters until the mother of the house protects him. Released, he crosses the cordillera into Chile on foot and horseback with nothing. It is the first of two exiles and the pattern of both.
suggested_refs: The estancia of the Rodríguez family outside San Luis, prison and improvised schoolroom

segments.name: The First Exile and the Charcoal

stops.name: Pocuro, the schoolmaster at thirteen pesos a month
stops.campa: On the Chilean side of the Andes, in the valley of Aconcagua, a village called Pocuro hires the destitute Argentine to keep its school for thirteen pesos a month. He is twenty. He teaches by day and reads by night whatever crosses the pass: Franklin's autobiography above all, which he will say made him wish to be Franklin. The exile's first employment on foreign ground is the trade he was born to and will never truly leave, whatever else he becomes: minister, general, ambassador, president. He is a schoolmaster who at intervals ran a country.
suggested_refs: The village school of Pocuro in the Aconcagua valley, his first paid classroom

stops.name: Valparaíso, the shop clerk and the English lessons
stops.campa: In the port he takes work as a shop assistant at half a wage, and spends a peso and a half of it on English lessons from an Englishman, plus the candle he burns reading past midnight. In six weeks he can read Scott; in a year and a half he has read sixty English volumes. He never learns to speak the language decently and never needs to. Valparaíso is where the provincial autodidact discovers that the world can be got at through print, and decides, permanently, that print is a public utility.
suggested_refs: The English lending libraries and printing houses of Valparaíso, his second university

stops.name: Copiapó, foreman at the mine of La Colorada
stops.campa: North, into the copper and silver desert of Atacama, where he serves nearly three years as mayordomo of the mine called La Colorada: keeping accounts, driving barreteros, learning by hand the geology and metallurgy he will one day legislate into schools of mines at San Juan and Catamarca. He reads in the galleries. He is a working manager of a real enterprise, which few of his lettered contemporaries ever were, and it marks his politics forever: he will always be more interested in a smelter than in a sonnet.
suggested_refs: The mine of La Colorada near Copiapó, in the Chilean mining north

stops.name: San Juan, El Zonda and the Colegio de Santa Rosa
stops.campa: Home at last, he founds two things in one year: a school for girls, the Colegio de Pensionistas de Santa Rosa de América, and a newspaper, El Zonda, printed on a press so poor that the whole paper is a single sheet. The school teaches young women in a province that has never educated any; the paper needles the federal governor until a punitive stamp tax kills it at six numbers. He has discovered his two permanent instruments, the classroom and the press, and that the second is the more dangerous.
suggested_refs: El Zonda, San Juan, 20 July 1839 — the first newspaper of the province, six numbers

stops.name: San Juan, the arrest and the beating
stops.campa: The federal reaction reaches Cuyo. He is seized in the street by the mazorca of Benavídez, struck about the head and face, and thrown into the cells; his mother and sisters petition, and he is released only on condition that he leave the country. He will carry the marks. His hatred of Rosas is not, from this night forward, a doctrine held at a distance but a personal quarrel between a beaten provincial schoolmaster and the man he holds responsible for every ignorance in the republic.
suggested_refs: The cells of San Juan under the governorship of Nazario Benavídez, November 1840

stops.name: Baños del Zonda, the charcoal on the wall
stops.campa: Riding out to the pass, the exile stops at the bathhouse in the Zonda gorge and writes on the wall in charcoal, beneath the arms of the republic, a sentence in French so that his pursuers will not read it: On ne tue point les idées. The government sends a commission to decipher the hieroglyph. Five years later the same words stand as the epigraph of Facundo, with his own Spanish rendering beside them: to men one cuts the throat; to ideas, not. He is wrong about the attribution, which he gives to Fortoul; he is not wrong about the proposition, and the ground has heard it first.
stops.quote: On ne tue point les idées.
stops.quote_source: Escrito con carbón en los Baños del Zonda, noviembre de 1840; llevado luego como epígrafe de Facundo (1845)
suggested_refs: The wall of the Baños del Zonda, San Juan, and the charcoal sentence that became the epigraph of Facundo
sources: Paul Verdevoye on the misattribution to Fortoul

segments.name: Santiago: the Method and the Book

stops.name: Valparaíso, the pen taken up at El Mercurio
stops.campa: An unknown foreigner walks into the offices of El Mercurio with an article on the anniversary of Chacabuco and walks out a journalist. Within months he is the most read and most detested pen in Chile: a man with no degree, no family, no country and no manners, writing about everything. He will edit or found El Progreso, El Heraldo Nacional, La Crónica. The Chilean decade makes him: it gives an exiled provincial the one thing San Juan could not, a public, and it teaches him that a newspaper is a portable republic.
suggested_refs: El Mercurio de Valparaíso, oldest Spanish-language daily still printing, where his first article appeared

stops.name: Santiago, the Escuela Normal de Preceptores
stops.campa: Manuel Montt, minister of instruction, gives the stateless journalist a state: the first teacher-training school in South America, and Sarmiento as its founding director. Twenty-eight students, a curriculum he writes himself, a manual for country schoolteachers, and a principle that will govern the rest of his life. Do not make schools by building rooms; make them by manufacturing teachers, a task of industrial scale. Everything from Paraná in 1870 to the kindergarten of 1884 descends from this room in Santiago.
suggested_refs: The Escuela Normal de Preceptores of Santiago, 14 June 1842, first normal school in South America
sources: Sarmiento, De la educación popular (1849), title page

stops.name: Santiago, the Memoria sobre ortografía americana
stops.campa: Before the Faculty of Humanities of the University of Chile, the man who learned to read from his mother proposes to reform the spelling of the Spanish language on American ground: one letter, one sound; abolish what the ear does not hear. Andrés Bello, the greatest grammarian in the hemisphere, receives him with courtesy and partial assent. Chile adopts a version of the reform and keeps it for decades. Sarmiento never fully abandons it, his own books print i for y, and the title page of the Viajes still says Africa i America.
suggested_refs: The Memoria sobre ortografía americana (1843) and the 'ortografía chilena' it produced

stops.name: Santiago, Facundo appears in the folletín of El Progreso
stops.campa: In serial instalments at the foot of a Santiago newspaper, and then as a book, appears Civilización i barbarie: vida de Juan Facundo Quiroga. It is biography, geography, polemic, prophecy and libel at once, written at speed to wreck a diplomatic mission of Rosas. It invents the Argentine literary tradition by accident. Its first move is to read the pampa as Asia: the ox-cart train as a camel caravan bound for Baghdad, the wagon-master as a caravan chief, the mounted raiders as Bedouin. The desert is the key, and the key is borrowed from the Orient.
stops.quote: Hay algo en las soledades argentinas que trae a la memoria las soledades asiáticas; alguna analogía encuentra el espíritu entre la pampa y las llanuras que median entre el Tigris y el Eúfrates.
stops.quote_source: Facundo, cap. I, 'Aspecto físico de la República Argentina' (1845)
suggested_refs: Facundo: civilización i barbarie (Imprenta del Progreso, Santiago, 1845), first edition
sources: Sarmiento, Facundo (1845), Introducción and cap. I
Wikipedia (es), 'Facundo o civilización y barbarie en las pampas argentinas'

stops.name: Santiago, the gaucho written as a Bedouin
stops.campa: The analogy hardens into a system. The tribe on the Asian steppe is the estancia; the caudillo is a Mahoma who could change the religion at will; the montonera that destroyed the cities of the interior is exactly the Bedouin horde now harrying the frontiers of French Algeria, same war, same men, same undisciplined strategy. He has never seen Africa. He is writing from a newspaper office in Santiago, out of Volney and the reviews, and he says so plainly. Within eighteen months he will be standing in that country, checking his own metaphor against the ground.
stops.quote: Las hordas beduinas que hoy importunan con su algazara y depredaciones las fronteras de la Argelia dan una idea exacta de la montonera argentina... La misma lucha de civilización y barbarie, de la ciudad y el desierto, existe hoy en África.
suggested_refs: Facundo, cap. IV: the montonera identified with the Bedouin horde on the Algerian frontier, written before he had seen Africa
sources: Sarmiento, Facundo (1845), caps. I, II, IV
Verified in the Spanish text: caps. I ('la vida de Abraham, que es la del beduino de hoy'), II, IV

stops.name: Valparaíso, embarkation on the government's commission
stops.campa: Chile is embarrassed by him and cannot spare him, so it sends him away usefully: a commission from Montt to inspect at first hand the primary-school systems of Europe and North America, funded by the state, with the rank of an official traveller. He sails at the end of October with letters of introduction and a plan to see everything. He is thirty-four, has never left the Southern Cone, and will be gone two and a half years. The letters he writes home become the Viajes por Europa, África i América.
suggested_refs: The commission of the Chilean Ministry of Public Instruction, 1845, to study primary education abroad
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes por Europa, África i América (1849-51), prologue

stops.name: Montevideo, the besieged city
stops.campa: The first letter of the Viajes is dated from a city under siege. Montevideo has been invested by Oribe and Rosas for three years and is held by a garrison of French, Italian and Argentine exiles; Garibaldi is in the harbour, the Argentine emigration is in the cafés, and Facundo is being read there before its author arrives. He finds his own reputation waiting for him on the wharf. The exile discovers that a book travels faster than a man, and that he has become, without a country, a public person.
suggested_refs: The Sitio Grande of Montevideo (1843-1851) and the Argentine emigration that sheltered there
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a Demetrio Peña, Montevideo, 14 de diciembre de 1845

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the slave empire
stops.campa: From the letter dated Rio, February 1846: a tropical capital of extraordinary beauty resting on a population of enslaved Africans, an emperor of twenty in a court of European manners, and a whole society that strikes him as a machine running on a fuel he considers morally and economically ruinous. He counts the numbers, as he always does. Brazil is his first sight of a plantation order at scale, and it sharpens the argument he will make for the rest of his life: that a country is made or unmade by the composition of its people.
suggested_refs: Rio de Janeiro under Pedro II, February 1846, the second letter of the Viajes
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a Miguel Piñero, Rio Janeiro, 20 de febrero de 1846

segments.name: Europe, and the Old Man at Grand Bourg

stops.name: Grand Bourg, a day alone with San Martín
stops.campa: An hour outside Paris, in a modest house by the Seine, lives the man who crossed the Andes, forgotten by the countries he made. Sarmiento is brought in by old friends' letters and given a whole day. He touches certain strings on purpose, a portrait of Bolívar noticed by chance, and watches the countryman of Grand Bourg vanish and the young general reappear, the bent back straightening, the small clouded eyes opening. Then they name Rosas, and the vision collapses: the old man defends the tyrant as the defender of American independence.
stops.quote: He pasado con él momentos sublimes, que quedarán para siempre grabados en mi espíritu. Solos un día entero... lo he visto transfigurarse, i desaparecer a mi vista el campagnard de Grandbourg i presentárseme el jeneral joven, que asoma sobre las cúspides de los Andes.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta a Antonino Aberastain, París, 4 de septiembre de 1846
suggested_refs: The house of José de San Martín at Grand Bourg, on the Seine near Évry
san_martin.journey.json (shared pin: the exile's house)
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a Antonino Aberastain, París, 4 de septiembre de 1846
Museo Histórico Sarmiento, 'Sarmiento visita a San Martín en Grand Bourg'

stops.name: Paris, the cunas and the salles d'asile
stops.campa: The commission is discharged on foot, school by school. A patroness of the Faubourg Saint-Germain, Madame Gresier, dresses down to the plainness of the nurses so as not to shame them, and guides him through the crèches and the infant asylums of Paris: hundreds of children in a yard, women in charge, reading and counting and singing and gymnastics before the age of six. He writes it all up for De la educación popular. This, not Froebel, is the first model of early schooling he carries back across the Atlantic.
stops.quote: Las Salas de Asilo, la más bella, la más útil y la más fecunda en resultados morales de todas las instituciones modernas.
suggested_refs: The Parisian salles d'asile and crèches of the 1840s, ancestors of the Argentine jardín de infantes
sources: Sarmiento, De la educación popular (1849), cap. sobre Cunas y Salas de Asilo

stops.name: Madrid, the reckoning with the mother country
stops.campa: The long letter to Lastarria from Madrid is the most brutal thing in the Viajes: a Spanish America settling accounts with Spain. He goes to the Teatro del Príncipe, sits in Romea's dressing room, and reports that in a week a foreigner can meet, and be on familiar terms with, every literary reputation in the country. Spain has produced no Byron, no Goethe, no Lamartine; the octosyllable of blind beggars is its measure. The bullfight appalls and fascinates him. He leaves convinced that the inheritance he must escape is Spanish.
stops.quote: Basta conocer un poco a Madrid para medir el alcance del drama español. Madrid, aunque real i mui noble, es siempre la villa de Madrid.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta a Victorino Lastarria, Madrid, 15 de noviembre de 1846
suggested_refs: The Teatro del Príncipe in Madrid, and the Casino de la calle del Príncipe, his whole survey of Spanish letters
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a V. Lastarria, Madrid, noviembre de 1846

stops.name: Orán, the letter from Africa begins
stops.campa: He has left Spain carrying letters to Marshal Bugeaud and a near-order to a consul to put him aboard the first warship going over. The African letter of the Viajes opens at Orán on the second of January, seventeen years into the French conquest and eleven months before the emir's surrender. This is a war zone, and he has arrived as an official guest of the army waging it. He is the only Latin American writer of his generation to walk into the Algerian war on purpose, to check a metaphor.
stops.quote: Ahora parto para África. Llevo cartas para el Mariscal Bugeaud, i una casi orden al Cónsul de Mallorca, para que me haga conducir a Arjel por el primer vapor de guerra que se presente.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde España, vísperas del paso a África (1846)
suggested_refs: The letter from Orán, 2 January 1847, opening the African section of the Viajes
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a Juan Thompson, Orán, 2 de enero de 1847

stops.name: The plain of the Mitidja, the colony and the fever
stops.campa: Behind Algiers spreads the Mitidja, the showpiece of French colonisation: Roman-looking roads, handsome new buildings, an apparent Europe transplanted. He is not fooled for a paragraph. Under the marsh lies malaria; the torrents off the Atlas erase a decade's work in an hour; a village of eight hundred has just been drowned overnight. And under the colony lies the country, unconverted. He is the same writer here as at home: the surface is civilisation, the substrate is the desert, and the substrate is patient.
stops.quote: El velado horizonte árabe está ahí siempre, i bajo sus anchos pliegues, un pueblo orijinal, un idioma primitivo, i una relijion intolerante... La tristeza habitual del grave semblante árabe está revelando, en su humildad aparente, ... la enerjia que no se somete, sino que aplaza para días mejores la venganza.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde África (Orán–Argel, enero de 1847)
suggested_refs: The Mitidja plain behind Algiers, model colony and malarial marsh
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a Juan Thompson, África, enero de 1847

stops.name: Argel, the prophecies and the name of Abd-el-Kader
stops.campa: He collects, and sets down in order, the Muslim prophecies of the Mahdi circulating in Algeria: the man from Sus-el-Aksa who will destroy Orán, camp four months in the Mitidja, and level Algiers; the year 1264 of the Hegira; the ninety no exegete can explain. He warns his correspondent not to take it lightly with a modern Christian's scepticism, for unbelief does not yet exist among the Arabs, and the emir would not be so great a warrior if he did not believe. The desert chieftain is a religious fact.
stops.quote: La palabra incredulidad no existe todavía entre los árabes, i Abd-El-Kader no fuera tan grande guerrero, si no creyera i esperara firmemente.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde África, sobre las profecías árabes (enero de 1847)
suggested_refs: The Mahdist prophecies current in Algeria in 1847, transcribed in the Viajes
abdelkader.journey.json (the emir as the Algerians' own believing warrior)
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a Juan Thompson, África, enero de 1847
Verified in the Spanish text of the Viajes (Obras, tomo V)

stops.name: Argel, Marshal Bugeaud and the mounted infantry
stops.campa: The governor-general receives him and talks shop. Bugeaud calls his engagements batallas ambulantes and explains his plan to mount infantry on mules to chase the Arab horse into the desert; he is delighted to hear that in America, on the pampa, they have done exactly that against the montoneras. Both men agree on the rule: to beat a barbarous people you must stay civilised, or you merely parody them. Two continents' counter-insurgencies compare notes across a table in Algiers, and each recognises the other.
stops.quote: El mariscal comprendió mui bien que los franceses parodiarían a los gauchos árabes, i que para vencer a un pueblo bárbaro es preciso conservarse civilizado.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde África, entrevista con el mariscal Bugeaud (enero de 1847)
suggested_refs: Marshal Thomas Bugeaud, governor-general of Algeria, and the razzia doctrine
abdelkader.journey.json (the same marshal, from the other side of the war)
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a Juan Thompson, África, enero de 1847
Verified in the Spanish text of the Viajes (Obras, tomo V)

stops.name: The duar, the diffa, and the tents of Abraham
stops.campa: Provided with a burnous for the dignity of his office, he rides out with an escort to a camp of tents to be given the ritual meal. Approaching the thorn circle he is seized by vertigo: Rebecca and Jael seem about to step out of the doorways. Then he sits down, crosses his legs, gets cramp, notices his hosts sprawling at their ease, hauls one knee up under his chin the way a gaucho does, and the vision dies. He knows this place. He has been here his whole life.
stops.quote: ¡Tate! me dije para mí, yo conozco todo esto, i las tiendas patriarcales de los descendientes de Abrahan no están mas avanzadas que los toldos de nuestros salvajes de las Pampas.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde África, la diffa en el duar (enero de 1847)
suggested_refs: The Arab duar and the diffa of hospitality, the scene in which Facundo's central metaphor was checked against the ground
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a Juan Thompson, África, enero de 1847
Verified in the Spanish text of the Viajes (Obras, tomo V)

stops.name: The plain of Eghris, the emir's father's house
stops.campa: General Arnault gallops him across the plain of Eghris outside Mascara. Here stands the paternal house of Abd-el-Kader, son of a great marabout to whom on pilgrimage at Mecca his son's destiny was revealed in a dream; here five thousand Arab horsemen gathered to proclaim him emir, in the manner, Sarmiento says, of Darius son of Hystaspes. He rides over the very field of the bay'a of 1832. That evening the general shows him a Revue des Deux Mondes and points at the title: Civilisation et Barbarie.
stops.quote: En aquella llanura está la casa paterna de Abd-El-Kader, hijo de un gran marabut, a quien en una peregrinación a la Meka le fueron revelados en sueños los altos destinos que estaban reservados a su hijo. Mas tarde en aquella misma llanura cinco mil jinetes árabes se reunieron para proclamar Emir a Abd-El-Kader.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde África, la llanura de Eghris cerca de Máscara (febrero de 1847)
suggested_refs: The plain of Eghris (Ghriss) near Mascara, where the tribes proclaimed Abd al-Qadir emir in 1832
abdelkader.journey.json (shared pin: 'Plain of Eghris, near Mascara — proclaimed Amir al-Mu'minin', 22 November 1832)
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a Juan Thompson, África, enero-febrero de 1847
Verified in the Spanish text of the Viajes (Obras, tomo V)
Charles de Mazade, review of Facundo, Revue des Deux Mondes (1846)

stops.name: Mascara, the Arab trackers and the limit of the world
stops.campa: At the general's table the talk is of desert scouts, and Sarmiento sits up: the Arab baqueanos are identical to the ones on the pampa. They smell the earth to take a bearing, taste the roots of grasses, read the paths. He concedes that the Arabs outdo his gauchos, they talk across two leagues and scent cattle at three, and gamely defends the honour of the rastreadores of home. Beyond Mascara, he writes, European life stops; barbarism and the desert begin, and there his journey round the civilised world ends.
stops.quote: Entre otras cosas los baqueanos árabes me llamaron la atención por la singular identidad con los nuestros de la Pampa. Como estos, huelen la tierra para orientarse, gustan las raíces de las yerbas, reconocen los senderos.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde África, en casa del jeneral Arnault, Máscara (febrero de 1847)
suggested_refs: The rastreador and the baqueano of Facundo, cap. II, recognised alive in the Algerian Sahara
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a Juan Thompson, África, enero-febrero de 1847
Sarmiento, Facundo (1845), cap. II ('El rastreador', 'El baqueano')

segments.name: Rome, and the Republic Without a Model

stops.name: Rome, the ruins and the sculptors
stops.campa: The letter from Rome is dated the sixth of April, in the brief liberal springtime of Pius IX before the revolutions. He walks the Campagna, now desert or vineyard; he sits in Tenerani's studio among the first sculptors of Europe and notes, with an American's arithmetic, that they are taking orders from Boston. Rome teaches him what a ruin is worth and what it costs, and he leaves it, as he leaves all of Europe, admiring the monuments and refusing the model.
suggested_refs: The studio of Pietro Tenerani in Rome, working on commissions from Boston
The Rome of Pius IX in the spring of 1847
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta desde Roma, 6 de abril de 1847

stops.name: New York, the drama without a plan
stops.campa: He lands from the Montezuma in September with almost no money and a fixed intention to dislike the place, and is overturned within weeks. The letter to Valentín Alsina that closes the Viajes is the hinge of his whole life: the United States, he writes, are a thing without any prior model, a kind of absurdity that shocks at first sight and frustrates expectation by fighting against received ideas. Everything Europe told him was impossible — a prosperous, literate, self-governing multitude — is here, running.
stops.quote: Los Estados Unidos son una cosa sin modelo anterior, una especie de disparate que choca a la primera vista, i frustra la espectación pugnando contra las ideas recibidas.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta a Valentín Alsina, Nueva York, 12 de noviembre de 1847
suggested_refs: The letter to Valentín Alsina, New York, 12 November 1847, closing the Viajes
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a Valentín Alsina, 12 de noviembre de 1847

stops.name: West Newton, Massachusetts, the house of Horace Mann
stops.campa: He goes to Massachusetts to find the man whose Report of an Educational Tour he has read in Chile: Horace Mann, secretary of the state board, architect of the common school. Mann has no Spanish and Sarmiento no English, so Mary Peabody Mann sits between them and translates for hours. The common school — free, universal, tax-supported, coeval with the founding of a village — is the answer he has been looking for since a lottery in San Juan in 1821. The friendship with Mary will outlive her husband by thirty years and reach Paraná.
stops.quote: Un hombre no llega a la plenitud de su desenvolvimiento moral e inteligente sino por la educación: luego la sociedad debe completar al padre en la crianza de su hijo.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta a Valentín Alsina, Nueva York, 12 de noviembre de 1847
suggested_refs: The Mann house at West Newton, Massachusetts, and the Massachusetts common school system
sources: Sarmiento, Viajes, carta a Valentín Alsina (1847)
Archivo General de la Nación, 'De Massachusetts a la Pampa'
Museo Histórico Sarmiento, epistolario Sarmiento–Mary Mann

stops.name: Santiago, De la educación popular
stops.campa: Back in Chile he discharges the commission in a single enormous book: a comparative anatomy of the school systems of France, Prussia, Holland, Britain and the United States, with costs, statistics, buildings, salaries, methods and furniture, addressed to governments that do not yet exist. The title page lists him as first director of the Escuela Normal de Santiago. De la educación popular is the blueprint; twenty years later he will be president of a country and will build from it, page by page, without changing the plan.
suggested_refs: De la educación popular (Santiago, Imprenta de Julio Belin, 1849)
sources: pestalozzi.journey.json, froebel.journey.json (the European method he is importing at second hand)

stops.name: Santiago, Recuerdos de provincia and Argirópolis
stops.campa: In one year he writes the two books that make him a candidate. Argirópolis proposes a federal capital on Martín García island and a united states of the Plata; Recuerdos de provincia answers a slander campaign by telling the story of his own family — the loom, the fig tree, the friar uncle, the mother — and thereby invents Argentine autobiography. He is manufacturing a public man out of a poor provincial's life, deliberately and in print, at the moment when Rosas is about to fall and someone will have to be ready.
suggested_refs: Recuerdos de provincia (Santiago, 1850) and Argirópolis (1850)

segments.name: The Sword, the Province, and the Legation

stops.name: Diamante, the Paraná crossed with the Ejército Grande
stops.campa: Urquiza rises against Rosas, and Sarmiento comes down from Chile to join him, as lieutenant-colonel, and above all as boletinero, keeping the army's press in a wagon so that the campaign will have a written account before it has a result. He crosses the Paraná at Diamante with twenty-four thousand men. He wears a French kepi and quarrels with everyone. The man who spent ten years arguing that the sword must serve the pen has arranged, characteristically, to carry both.
suggested_refs: The crossing of the Paraná at Diamante by the Ejército Grande, December 1851
sources: Sarmiento, Campaña en el Ejército Grande (1852)

stops.name: Caseros, the victory and the quarrel
stops.campa: Rosas is destroyed in a morning on the plain by the Palomar de Caseros and rides away to a farm in Hampshire. Within days Sarmiento has broken with the victor: Urquiza is a caudillo too, a chieftain with a red band, and the boletinero says so in print and leaves for Chile in disgust to write Campaña en el Ejército Grande as an open letter of accusation. Twenty years of desired revolution, achieved and repudiated in a fortnight. He would rather be right than governing, until he is.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Caseros, 3 February 1852, and the Campaña en el Ejército Grande (1852)
sources: Sarmiento, Campaña en el Ejército Grande (1852)

stops.name: Olta, the head of the Chacho
stops.campa: Governor of his own province and director of the war against the montonera of La Rioja, he presides over the pursuit of Ángel Vicente Peñaloza, the Chacho, who is run down at Olta, killed with a lance, and beheaded, his head set on a pike in the plaza of San Juan Bautista de Olta. Two years earlier Sarmiento had written to Mitre the sentence that will follow him forever: do not try to economise gaucho blood. The book that read the caudillo as a desert chieftain has become a government that treats him as one.
stops.quote: No trate de economizar sangre de gauchos. Este es un abono que es preciso hacer útil al país.
stops.quote_source: Carta de Sarmiento a Bartolomé Mitre, Buenos Aires, 20 de septiembre de 1861
suggested_refs: The place of the killing of Ángel Vicente Peñaloza at Olta, La Rioja, 12 November 1863
sources: Carta a Bartolomé Mitre, 20 de septiembre de 1861
José Hernández, Vida del Chacho (1863), the answering account

stops.name: New York, the legation and the loss of Dominguito
stops.campa: Minister plenipotentiary to the United States, he spends three years measuring a republic in mid-reconstruction, receives an honorary doctorate at Ann Arbor, corresponds with Mary Mann, who is translating Facundo into English, and is elected president of Argentina without campaigning, from abroad. In the middle of it comes the telegram: his adopted son Domingo Fidel, twenty-one, has fallen in the assault at Curupaytí in Paraguay. He writes the boy's life as a book. The war he will inherit has already taken the only son he had.
suggested_refs: Life in the Argentine Republic in the Days of the Tyrants, Mary Mann's translation of Facundo (New York, 1868)
Sarmiento, Vida de Dominguito (1886)
sources: Museo Histórico Sarmiento, epistolario Sarmiento–Mary Mann

segments.name: The Presidency and the Last River

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the oath of office
stops.campa: He comes ashore from the legation and is sworn in as president of a country he has spent most of his adult life outside of. The programme was written in 1849 and has not changed: schools, immigrants, railways, telegraph, statistics, an observatory, a navy. He inherits a war in Paraguay he did not want, a rebellion in Entre Ríos, and a treasury with nothing in it. The schoolmaster of Pocuro, who once earned thirteen pesos a month, now has a state to build the schoolhouse with.
suggested_refs: The presidency of Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, 12 October 1868 – 12 October 1874

stops.name: Paraná, the Escuela Normal and the teachers from the north
stops.campa: He signs the decree founding the first national normal school of Argentina at Paraná, which will open its doors the August after next; and to staff the system he sends for teachers from the United States: sixty-five women and a handful of men, recruited largely through Mary Mann, who cross an ocean to Entre Ríos, Tucumán, Catamarca, San Juan, learning Spanish as they go. Some die of fever, most stay for life. It is the largest deliberate import of pedagogy in the hemisphere's history, and it is the Massachusetts common school, and behind that the Swiss method, arriving in the Río de la Plata.
suggested_refs: The Escuela Normal de Paraná (1870) and the sixty-five North American teachers
pestalozzi.journey.json (the method's source), froebel.journey.json (its early-childhood branch)
sources: Museo Histórico Sarmiento, 'Creación de la Escuela Normal de Paraná'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the yellow fever
stops.campa: Yellow fever takes some fourteen thousand people out of a city of under two hundred thousand; the government dissolves, the rich abandon San Telmo forever and move north, and carts collect the dead. Sarmiento is criticised for leaving the capital and never lives it down. Out of the catastrophe come the things he actually believed in: a new cemetery at Chacarita, and the beginning of the water and drainage works that end the epidemic era. The statistician's republic is founded on a plague pit.
suggested_refs: The Cementerio de la Chacarita, opened in the fever of 1871
The 1871 yellow fever epidemic of Buenos Aires
sources: Wikipedia (es), 'Epidemia de fiebre amarilla en Buenos Aires de 1871'

stops.name: Córdoba, the Observatorio Astronómico
stops.campa: He brings Benjamin Gould from Cambridge to build an observatory in Córdoba and Germán Burmeister to found an academy of sciences beside it, and he inaugurates the dome himself. From it will come the Uranometría Argentina and the Córdoba Durchmusterung, the first systematic mapping of the southern sky, catalogued from a provincial city of the interior. The man who read the pampa as a desert of ignorance answers it, finally, by pointing an instrument at the part of heaven Europe cannot see.
suggested_refs: The Observatorio Nacional Argentino at Córdoba (1871) and Gould's Uranometría Argentina
The Academia Nacional de Ciencias de Córdoba under Germán Burmeister

stops.name: Paraná, the first jardín de infantes
stops.campa: Thirty-five children between three and six are enrolled in the kindergarten annexed to the normal school at Paraná, organised and directed by Sara Chamberlain de Eccleston, one of the North American teachers he brought over. She founds the Argentine Froebelian Society and translates the manuals of the Gifts. The idea reached Sarmiento through Mary Mann and the Peabody sisters; it reaches Entre Ríos through a widow from Philadelphia. Froebel comes to the Plata by way of Boston, forty years after Blankenburg, and the old man is alive to see it.
suggested_refs: The kindergarten of the Escuela Normal de Paraná, 4 August 1884, first in Argentina
froebel.journey.json (the Gifts and the name of the kindergarten)
sources: Buenos Aires Ciudad, 'Huellas maestras: Sarah Chamberlin de Eccleston'

stops.name: Asunción, the death on the river
stops.campa: Old, deaf, asthmatic and out of office, he goes up the river to Asunción for the warmth and stays to work: schools, a newspaper, contracts for more teachers, eucalyptus and willow planted in the Paraguayan heat. He dies there of heart failure on the eleventh of September, seventy-seven years old, in the capital of the country his own government helped destroy, on the far side of a river, in exile one last time by choice. The state that carried him home is the state he built.
suggested_refs: The Casa de Sarmiento in Asunción, Paraguay, where he died on 11 September 1888

stops.name: Recoleta, the return of the body
stops.campa: The body comes down the Paraná by steamer, met at every port by schoolchildren, and is buried in the Recoleta ten days after the death. Carlos Pellegrini speaks the sentence the country has kept: that this was the most powerful brain America has produced. The eleventh of September becomes the Day of the Teacher across the hemisphere. He wanted no monument but a school, and got both: an obelisk of a tomb, and by the last count of his life more than a thousand eight hundred schoolhouses.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Sarmiento in the Cementerio de la Recoleta, Buenos Aires
El Día del Maestro, 11 September, kept across Spanish America
